b: You can get this blog delivered to you every day, for free. The details are here: https://seths.blog/subscribe/
You can subscribe to streaming channels like Dropout (a new unscripted game show every time), MHz or RetroCrush (rare anime).
You can subscribe to Apocabox if you’re a prepper in need of more stuff, or History by Mail, which will send you facsimiles of historical documents.
And of course, you can subscribe to Elle Cordova on YouTube.
But why? In an instant-on, find-what-you-want world, why spend the time or the money?

The immediate one is that subscriptions are an asset and a signal. The creator of the product or service is more likely to do the work you seek if you give them a reliable way to get the work out there. This is why Google and others fight so hard to break the connection–they want to own your attention instead.

The long-term one is that the arrival of your subscription is a prompt. It shows up on its schedule, not yours. It’s not just a reminder, it creates a pattern. Seventy years ago, a stack of Readers Digest or National Geographic magazines was a signal to visitors and to the homeowner as well. The same for the New Yorker twenty years ago. And not just for the cartoons.

If you’re already a subscriber to the blog, thanks. If it hasn’t been getting to you, please check your promo folder or resubscribe. And mostly, please forward this to someone who might want to join in. When your colleagues subscribe too, you have a shared prompt to riff on.

My RSS reader is a treasure box of hundreds of subscriptions. The blog posts and the occasional XKCD have enriched my life and knowing that more will come opens up anticipation and creativity on my part.
